questions.question: Explain the effects of intrinsic and extrinsic motivation on athlete performance. [U] [1,2]
questions.solution_html:
• Answer: Intrinsic motivation arises from internal factors, such as a love for the game or personal
  • satisfaction, and often results in greater persistence, creativity, and resilience, sustaining long-term
  • engagement. In contrast, extrinsic motivation is driven by external rewards or recognition, which can be
  • powerful but may not sustain performance in the long term. Relying only on extrinsic factors may lead to
  • burnout or a decline in motivation if those rewards are absent.

questions.question: Explain how sports fandom can lead to tribalism and divisiveness. / [CO2]

• Need for Belonging and Identity: Humans have an innate need to belong to groups for a sense
  • of community, meaning, and security.
  • Social Identity Theory : This theory explains that individuals derive part of their self -worth and
  • self-esteem from their group memberships. To maintain a positive self -image, fans often highlight

  • Basking in Reflected Glory (BIRGing): Fans boost their self- esteem by associating themselves

  • Out-group Hostility: Intense loyalty to one's own group naturally leads to rivalry and sometimes

questions.question: What is achievement behavior in sports? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Achievement behavior is primarily discussed within the framework of achievement motivation
  • theory. Definition: Achievement motivation is a person's desire to strive for satisfaction when
  • making comparisons with some standard of excellence.
  • A central tenet is that behavior have influence on athlete's personality (trait- centered view) or the
  • situation itself (situation-centered view).
  • Need Achievement Theory: explain how personality traits and situational demands combine to
  • shape an athlete's emotional responses and drive behavior. It posits that people are motivated by
  • either a desire for success or a fear of failure.
  • Achievement Goal Theory (AGT): identifies two primary goal orientations:
  • Task/Mastery Orientation: Athletes focus on self -improvement, mastering the skill, and achieving
  • personal bests (e.g., a personal best in running).
  • Ego/Outcome Orientation: Athletes focus on outperforming others and winning. Success is defined
  • by social comparison. This can be less stable and more prone to negative emotions (anxiety) if the
  • athlete perceives their ability as low or faces a superior opponent.

questions.question: How does the brain’s reward system affect motivation behaviour in athletes? / [CO1] [8x2=16] Part D Long Answer Type Questions Each Question carries 7 marks
questions.solution_html:
• The brain's reward system affects motivation in athletics by using dopamine pathways to
  • reinforce behaviors that lead to positive outcomes, such as achieving goals, receiving social
  • approval, and experiencing the intrinsic satisfaction of exercise.
  • Dopamine Release and Reinforcement: The brain's reward system, releases dopamine in response
  • to rewarding experiences. In an athletic context, this happens when an athlete achieves a personal
  • best wins a competition, or even just completes a tough training session. This surge of dopamine
  • creates a sense of pleasure and reinforces the behavior, making the athlete want to repeat the activity.
  • Goal-Directed Action (Motivation): The prospect of a future reward (e.g., winning a medal,
  • improving performance) is a strong motivator. Social recognition, such as praise from a coach,
  • applause from a crowd, or peer acceptance, also activates the same reward circuits as more tangible
  • rewards.

questions.question: Evaluate why psychology is used in sports. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Psychology is used in sports because human performance is influenced not only by physical
  • abilities but also by mental and emotional factors. One major reason psychology is used in sports
  • is to enhance performance. Psychological skills such as imagery, goal setting, and positive self -
  • talk help athletes sharpen their mental focus and improve execution of skills during
  • competition.Another important area is managing stress and anxiety. Sport psychology teaches
  • athletes techniques for relaxation, breathing control, and cognitive restructuring, helping them stay
  • calm and composed even in high- pressure moments. Motivation is another key factor studied in
  • sport psychology. Athletes need strong motivation to persist through long training hours, injuries,
  • setbacks, and competition failures.
  • Psychology also plays a role in helping athletes regulate their emotions. Learning emotional control
  • improves concentration, decision- making, and overall consistency.Another important use of
  • psychology is improving focus and attention. Training attention helps them block out distractions
  • such as crowd noise, pressure, or negative thoughts, which is essential for skill execution.
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025

questions.question: Explain the role of perceived competence in influencing motivation and performance in athletes, and discuss how task-oriented and ego-oriented athletes differ in this regard. / [CO2] [2x7=14]
questions.solution_html:
• Perceived competence refers to an athlete’s belief in their ability to perform successfully in a
  • sport situation. This concept is best explained through Achievement Goal Theory, proposed by
  • Nicholls. When athletes feel competent, they experience higher intrinsic motivation, take on
  • challenging tasks, and show persistence even during setbacks. This leads to better focus, lower
  • anxiety, and improved performance.
  • Achievement Goal Theory states that athletes adopt two main orientations: task-oriented and ego-
  • oriented. These orientations influence how they evaluate their competence.
  • Task-oriented athlete s judge their competence based on personal improvement, learning, and
  • effort. They focus on mastering skills rather than comparing themselves with others. Because their
  • perception of competence depends on internal standards, it remains stable even when they face
  • strong opponents or experience failure. As a result, task -oriented athletes stay motivated, persist
  • longer, enjoy their sport more, and experience lower anxiety. They view challenges as opportunities
  • for growth.
  • Ego-oriented athletes, o n the other hand, judge their competence by comparing themselves to
  • others. For them, success means outperforming opponents or being seen as talented. Their perceived
  • competence depends on external comparisons, which makes it fragile. When ego -oriented athletes
  • believe they can win, their motivation is high. However, when they face stronger competitors or fear
  • being outperformed, their perceived competence decreases quickly. This can lead to anxiety,
  • avoidance of challenging tasks, a nd inconsistent performance. They may even choose easier tasks
  • to protect their image of ability.
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025
